729.title: Speak, for I hear (1 Samuel 3)
729.hook: the boy hears his name at night and answers "Speak; for Thy servant heareth"
729.howItsDone: Jews read Samuel's night call as part of the Former Prophets, and the boy's answer, speak, for thy servant heareth, is read as a picture of what it means to listen for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah's song: the mighty falling, the poor lifted and seated among princes. Your line was raised from the dust. Today, her son, asleep in the sanctuary.

It's night in the sanctuary at Shiloh. The old priest Eli is lying down in his place; his eyes have grown dim. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. And the boy Samuel is asleep near the ark. Then a voice says his name. Samuel. He runs to Eli: here am I, you called me. I didn't call, says Eli; lie down again. The voice comes again. He runs again. And the text slips in why: Samuel did not yet know the LORD. He's hearing a voice he has no way to recognize.
screen: `NIGHT. THE LAMP STILL BURNS.` → `HERE AM I, YOU CALLED ME.` → `HE DIDN'T KNOW THE VOICE YET.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens by setting the scene: in those days the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were not common. So when it finally comes, it comes to a boy who can't tell it from an old man's voice. When the call comes a third time, Eli understands. And the old priest does this well. He doesn't take over. He teaches the boy one sentence and sends him back to bed: if you are called, say, Speak, LORD; for Thy servant heareth. The LORD came and stood, the text says, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. And Samuel answers, "Speak; for Thy servant heareth." The answer isn't a request. Not, give me a sign. It's, I'm here, I'm listening, go ahead. And what he hears is hard: judgment on Eli's own house, and his sons. Samuel lies there until morning, afraid to tell the man who raised him. Eli makes him tell everything, and hide nothing, and answers: it is the LORD; let him do what seems good to him. So the night has two listeners: a boy learning to say speak, and an old man who hears bad news about himself and doesn't look away. The chapter ends with Samuel growing up, and the LORD letting none of his words fall to the ground. The rare word isn't rare anymore.
screen: `THE WORD WAS RARE IN THOSE DAYS.` · `ELI TEACHES HIM ONE SENTENCE.` · `A HARD MESSAGE, TOLD WHOLE.` · `NONE OF HIS WORDS FELL TO THE GROUND.` · then, large: `SPEAK; FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie still, with the lights down if you can, and listen without asking for anything: the fridge, a car, your own breath, your thoughts as they come. If something keeps coming back, a name, a worry, let it come. If you pray, say Samuel's words, speak, for thy servant heareth, and stay quiet; if you don't, simply say to yourself: I'm listening.
Speak. The word Samuel says in the dark at Shiloh, taught to him by Eli, after he'd heard his name called three times.
Your line: here am I. The listening came before the message. Day seven hundred twenty-nine, done.

730.title: The glory departed (1 Samuel 4)
730.hook: the ark is captured, Eli dies, and a baby is named "the glory is departed"
730.howItsDone: Jews read the loss of the ark at Aphek as part of the Former Prophets, and some readers take the elders' plan to carry the ark into battle as a warning against treating holy things as charms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, speak: a boy in the dark at Shiloh, learning to answer. Your line was here am I. Today, the hard message comes true.

A runner comes from the battlefield with his clothes torn and earth on his head, and the whole city cries out. Eli, very old now, his eyes set so that he cannot see, sits on his seat by the road, waiting. His heart, the text says, trembled for the ark of God. Israel had lost a battle to the Philistines, and the elders had a plan: bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh into the camp, so that it may come among us and save us. When it arrived, the soldiers shouted until the earth rang. Now the runner reaches the old man. Israel has fled. Your two sons are dead. And the ark of God is taken.
screen: `A RUNNER WITH EARTH ON HIS HEAD.` → `BRING THE ARK, IT WILL SAVE US.` → `THE ARK OF GOD IS TAKEN.`

segments.voice: It's the ark that breaks him. When the runner names the ark, Eli falls backward from his seat by the gate, his neck breaks, and he dies. Then the chapter turns somewhere unexpected: not to the generals or the priests, but to a woman in labor. The wife of Eli's son Phinehas hears it all at once: the ark taken, her father-in-law dead, her husband dead. The labor comes on her suddenly. The women attending her try to comfort her: fear not, you've borne a son. She doesn't answer, and doesn't take it to heart. She has one thing left to do. She names the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory is departed from Israel," because the ark was taken, and because of her father-in-law and her husband. Then she says it again: the glory is departed from Israel; for the ark of God is taken. The elders carried the ark into battle so it would save them. It didn't. The chapter doesn't soften it. In one day the ark is gone, the old priest is dead with his two sons, and the one who names it plainly is a dying mother, giving her son a name nobody would want. And yet the book doesn't end here. In the chapters that follow, the ark's story goes on, and not the way the Philistines expected.
screen: `THE ARK CARRIED INTO BATTLE.` · `ELI FALLS AT THE GATE.` · `A MOTHER NAMES WHAT WAS LOST.` · `THE STORY DOESN'T END HERE.` · then, large: `THE GLORY IS DEPARTED FROM ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Let a loss of something bigger than you come to mind: a place that closed, a community that broke apart, a hope you carried for years. Don't rush to the bright side; give it a true name, even just in your head, and let the naming be enough for now. If you pray, bring that loss to God exactly as it is.
Ichabod. The name a dying mother gives her son on the day the ark is taken and Eli dies: the glory is departed from Israel.
Your line: name it plainly. The bright side can wait a while. See you tomorrow.

731.title: Like all the nations (1 Samuel 8)
731.hook: the people ask for a king like everyone else, and Samuel warns them
731.howItsDone: Jewish commentators differ on this chapter: some read the request for a king as wrong in itself, others read Deuteronomy as allowing a king and fault only the people's motive, to be like the nations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ichabod, the name a mother gave her son: the glory is departed. Your line was name it plainly. Today, years later, the people want something new.

The elders of Israel gather at Samuel's home in Ramah, and they put it plainly. Samuel has judged Israel for a lifetime, going round a circuit from town to town, and he has made his sons judges after him. It hasn't worked. His sons, the text says, did not walk in his ways. They turned aside after gain, took bribes, and bent justice. So: you are old, and your sons don't walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us, like all the nations.
screen: `SAMUEL IS OLD.` → `HIS SONS TAKE BRIBES.` → `MAKE US A KING.`

segments.voice: Their complaint is fair; the text says so before they do. But listen to the last phrase. Not just, give us a better judge. Like all the nations. They want to look like everyone around them. The thing displeases Samuel, and he prays. The answer is surprising. Listen to the people, God tells him: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me, that I should not be king over them. Still, give them what they ask. But warn them first. So Samuel tells them what a king will do. He will take your sons for his chariots and his horsemen, to plow his ground and reap his harvest and make his weapons. He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks and bakers. He'll take your best fields and vineyards for his servants, and a tenth of your grain and your flocks. Take, and take, and take. And you'll be his servants, and you'll cry out on that day because of the king you chose. The people answer: no; but we will have a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles. They've heard the cost, and they still want it. God tells Samuel: listen to their voice, and make them a king. Some readers hear a warning about power here. Others hear how badly people can want to be like everyone else.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting lately, a phone, a job title, a kind of life, and ask Samuel's question gently: what will it take from me? Then ask the elders' question honestly: do I want it because it's good, or because everyone around me has one?

732.title: Hidden among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:20–24)
732.hook: the tall new king hides from his own crowning
732.howItsDone: Jews read Saul's choosing at Mizpah as part of the Former Prophets; commentators differ on whether his hiding shows humility or fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elders asking Samuel for a king, like all the nations. Your line was take, and take, and take. Today, they get their king, if they can find him.

The whole people is gathered at Mizpah, and Samuel names a king by lot, so everyone can watch it narrow down. The tribes come near, and the tribe of Benjamin is taken. Then the family of the Matrites. Then one man: Saul, the son of Kish. Every eye turns to find him, and he isn't there. They look. They call. Nothing. So they ask the LORD: has the man come here yet? And the answer comes back: "Behold, he hath hid himself among the baggage."
screen: `BENJAMIN IS TAKEN.` → `SAUL, SON OF KISH.` → `AND HE ISN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's what makes it strange: Saul already knows. Samuel had taken him aside on the edge of town, poured oil on his head, and told him God had chosen him. When Saul went home and his uncle asked what Samuel had said, Saul told him about the lost donkeys he'd been chasing, and nothing about the kingdom. And before any of that, when Samuel first hinted at it, Saul said: am I not a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and isn't my family the least of them all? Gideon said much the same, down in his winepress. So the lot can hardly surprise him. And he's hiding among the gear, the bags and supplies people brought. The tallest man in Israel, crouched behind the luggage. The people run and fetch him, and when he stands among them, he's higher than any of them from his shoulders upward. Samuel says: do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There's none like him. The people shout: long live the king. But not everyone. Some worthless men say, how shall this man save us? They despise him and bring him no gift. And Saul, the text says, held his peace. Readers hear his hiding in different ways: humility, a man who didn't want power, or fear, a man who knew how heavy it would be. The text doesn't decide. It shows a man who looked like a king from the outside, crouched where no one could see him.

segments.voice: Think of something you've been asked to do, or know you're meant to do, that you keep ducking, leading something, speaking up, being the grown-up in a hard family moment, and notice where you've been hiding: busyness, jokes, the luggage. Don't force a decision; just stand up from behind the bags in your mind, and let yourself be seen. If you pray, ask for the strength to stand.

733.title: To obey is better (1 Samuel 15:22)
733.hook: "to obey is better than sacrifice"; Saul chose the showy offering
733.tomorrow: The Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7)
733.howItsDone: Jews read Saul's war with Amalek as part of the Former Prophets, and Samuel's line that to obey is better than sacrifice is studied as a teaching about what God asks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saul, the tall new king crouched behind the luggage at Mizpah. Your line was he hid among the baggage. Today, Saul is king, and he's not hiding anymore.

"Blessed be thou of the LORD; I have performed the commandment of the LORD." That's how Saul greets Samuel, back from war against Amalek. Job done, as far as he's concerned. On the way home he has even set up a monument for himself at Carmel. Samuel asks one quiet question. What then is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and the lowing of oxen that I hear? Saul had been told to leave nothing of Amalek's, and here are the best of the sheep and cattle, alive, bleating in the background of his victory speech.
screen: `I HAVE PERFORMED THE COMMANDMENT.` → `A MONUMENT AT CARMEL.` → `WHAT IS THIS BLEATING OF SHEEP?`

segments.voice: Saul has an answer ready. The people spared the best of the sheep and oxen, he says, to sacrifice to the LORD your God; the rest we destroyed. The command against Amalek is hard to read, a command to destroy everything, and this lesson won't pretend otherwise. But the chapter's own question is narrower: Saul was told one thing, did another, then dressed it up as worship. Samuel answers. Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt-offerings and sacrifices, as in hearkening to his voice? "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." To obey, and to hearken. In Hebrew, the word for obey here is the verb for hear, the same verb as in Shema, hear, O Israel. A few days ago, a boy in the sanctuary said speak, for thy servant heareth. Now a king is told that hearing is worth more than the fattest offering. Then Saul admits it: I have sinned, because I feared the people, and hearkened to their voice. He did hearken, just to the wrong voice. And as Samuel turns to go, Saul asks: honor me now, I pray, before the elders of my people. Even his apology wants an audience. The prophet Hosea sounds a similar note later: God desires mercy, and not sacrifice. But here it's one king, a monument, and some bleating sheep he hoped no one would hear.
screen: `THE BEST WAS SAVED FOR SACRIFICE.` · `OBEY MEANS HEAR.` · `I FEARED THE PEOPLE.` · `HONOR ME BEFORE THE ELDERS.` · then, large: `TO OBEY IS BETTER THAN SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Think of one plain thing someone has actually asked of you lately, a partner, a parent, a friend, your own body: the dishes, the phone call, the apology without a speech. Notice whether part of you would rather make a grander gesture, and choose the plain thing. If you pray, hold Samuel's words: to obey is better than sacrifice.
Shema. The Hebrew verb for hear and obey, the same word Samuel used when he told Saul that obeying is worth more than the fattest offering.
Your line: do the plain thing. No monument needed, and no audience. Day seven hundred thirty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 733 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.`

734.title: The Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7)
734.hook: the youngest shepherd is chosen, not the tall brothers
734.howItsDone: Jews read David's anointing in Bethlehem as part of the Former Prophets, and the line that God looks on the heart is studied as a teaching about not judging by appearances.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shema, to hear, the verb Samuel used: to obey is better than sacrifice. Your line was do the plain thing. Today, Samuel goes looking for the next king.

A horn of oil, and a dangerous errand. Samuel is sent to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, because God has chosen a king from among his sons. Samuel is afraid: if Saul hears, he'll kill me. So he goes with a heifer to offer a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and his sons. The first son walks in, Eliab, the eldest, and Samuel thinks: surely this is the one. He looks like a king. Last time, Israel got a king who stood head and shoulders above everyone. This must be him.
screen: `A HORN OF OIL, TO BETHLEHEM.` → `ELIAB WALKS IN.` → `SURELY THIS IS THE ONE.`

segments.voice: And God says no. Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. Then the line the chapter turns on: "for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Even a prophet, even Samuel, judged by height. Jesse brings the next son, Abinadab. Not this one. Then Shammah. Not this one. Jesse makes seven of his sons pass before Samuel, and to each the answer is the same: the LORD has not chosen these. So Samuel asks, almost funnily: are these all your children? Well, says Jesse, there's still the youngest. He's out keeping the sheep. Nobody thought to call him in. Send and fetch him, Samuel says; we won't sit down until he comes. So everyone waits, standing, for a boy to come in from the field. And when David arrives, the text describes him: ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and good to look at. The same chapter that says don't look at appearances tells us he was handsome. Some readers find a little joke in that: the point was never that looks are bad, only that they aren't what God goes by. Arise, anoint him, God says, for this is he. Samuel anoints him in the middle of his brothers, and the spirit of the LORD comes on David from that day forward. The brothers in the room are passed over; the one left in the field is chosen.
screen: `EVEN SAMUEL JUDGED BY HEIGHT.` · `SEVEN SONS, AND NOT THESE.` · `THE YOUNGEST, OUT WITH THE SHEEP.` · `HANDSOME TOO, AND THAT'S NOT WHY.` · then, large: `THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've sized up by how they look, sound or dress, or what they do for work: a coworker, a neighbor, maybe you, in the mirror. Set the outside aside and ask: what do I actually know about their heart, and what have they carried? If you don't know, just notice that; if you pray, hold Samuel's lesson: the LORD looketh on the heart.
David. The youngest son left out in the field, ruddy and good to look at, chosen because God looks on the heart, not the height.
Your line: the heart, not the height. Even Samuel had to learn it. See you tomorrow.

735.title: David's harp (1 Samuel 16:14–23)
735.hook: David plays and Saul's dark mood lifts
735.howItsDone: Jews read David's playing for Saul as part of the Former Prophets; by tradition, David is also linked with the book of Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David, the youngest son, called in from the sheep and anointed in Bethlehem. Your line was the heart, not the height. Today, the same chapter, in the palace.

One verse says the spirit of the LORD came on David. The very next says it left Saul. And something else comes instead. The text calls it an evil spirit from the LORD, and it terrifies him. The king is in the dark, and his servants can see it. So they suggest what people still suggest for someone who's low: let us look for a man who can play the harp. When the dark comes on you, he'll play with his hand, and you'll be well. Saul says yes. Find me someone who plays well.
screen: `THE SPIRIT LEAVES SAUL.` → `THE KING IS IN THE DARK.` → `FIND SOMEONE WHO CAN PLAY.`

segments.voice: One of the young men says: I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, skillful in playing, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, prudent, good-looking, and the LORD is with him. So Saul sends to Jesse for David, who is with the sheep, and Jesse loads a donkey with bread, a skin of wine and a young goat, and sends his youngest son to the king. Nothing in the text says Saul knows what happened in Bethlehem, where this boy was just anointed with oil among his brothers. David walks into the palace not as a rival, but as a musician, to help the man whose throne he'll one day sit on. And the text is tender: Saul loved him greatly, and David became his armor-bearer. Let David stay with me, Saul sends word, for he has found favor in my sight. The chapter ends with a picture. Whenever the spirit from God was upon Saul, David took the harp and played with his hand, and Saul found relief, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him. The Hebrew word for this harp is kinnor, a stringed instrument. The book doesn't say what he played, or whether there were words. Just that someone played when the dark came, and the king was well. This week, a boy said speak, a mother named what was lost, a people asked for a king, a king hid and then kept the showy offering, and a shepherd was chosen for his heart. Today that shepherd sits down beside the king, and plays.
screen: `A SON OF JESSE WHO CAN PLAY.` · `THE RIVAL WALKS IN AS A HELPER.` · `SAUL LOVED HIM GREATLY.` · `THE DARK SPIRIT DEPARTED.` · then, large: `DAVID TOOK THE HARP, AND PLAYED WITH HIS HAND.`

David's harp. The kinnor the young shepherd played for Saul, so that when the dark came, the king was refreshed and well.
